strengths: The paper addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: converting sparse, multi-date satellite imagery into explorable urban scenes without scene-specific street-level observations. The combination of satellite-grounded structure and pretrained generative priors is practically appealing.

The pipeline is coherent and well motivated. Appearance modeling addresses temporal variation, while progressively lowering refinement viewpoints provides a sensible curriculum for completing increasingly occluded regions.

The reported perceptual improvements are substantial. On DFC2019, FIDCLIP improves from 87.19 for Mip-Splatting to 27.35; on GoogleEarth, it improves from 28.73 for GaussianCity to 9.91. Figures 6 and 11–12 show visibly clearer facades and fewer artifacts. GoogleEarth pixel-level results provide complementary evidence beyond distribution metrics.

Evaluation includes satellite reconstruction and city-generation baselines, eight quantitatively evaluated scenes, additional qualitative scenes, and user studies with 89 participants each. Ablations support the usefulness of the curriculum and multiple diffusion samples, although their scope is limited.

The supplement provides substantial implementation detail, including prompts, camera schedules, optimization settings, and training costs. The paper also appropriately acknowledges computational expense and degraded street-level textures.
weaknesses: The depth objective is technically inconsistent with its stated purpose. Equation (3) defines the loss as the absolute Pearson correlation, and Equations (4)–(5) minimize it with positive weight. This encourages uncorrelated depths rather than agreement. This may be a manuscript error, but the implemented objective must be clarified before the depth-supervision results are reproducible; a corrected equation alone would not establish which objective produced the experiments.

The evidence supports perceptual synthesis more strongly than the repeated claims of geometric accuracy and cross-view consistency. CLIP-based distribution metrics and visual preference do not establish accurate recovered geometry, particularly for hallucinated facades. There is no direct depth/surface evaluation, reprojection-consistency measurement, or quantitative assessment of geometry preservation after refinement. Such evidence could be obtained on the controlled GoogleEarth setup without requiring unknowable real facade textures.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the incremental contribution needs stronger isolation. Most components are adopted from existing methods, including WildGaussians-style appearance modeling, monocular-depth supervision, FlowEdit, and iterative dataset updates. The central curriculum and sampling choices are tested on only JAX_068, without uncertainty estimates or clearly compute-matched controls. A closely matched diffusion-refinement baseline using the same initialization and optimization budget would better establish the contribution beyond integrating existing components.

The evaluation protocol has material ambiguities. Section 4.1 does not clearly specify patch overlap, rendering resolution, or whether the reported 4,320/3,456 patch counts are per scene or pooled. These patches originate from only 30/24 frames per scene and are highly correlated; scene-level uncertainty is absent. Moreover, the claim of outperforming every baseline on every metric is contradicted by DFC2019 SSIM: CoR-GS scores 0.350 versus 0.321 for the proposed method.

The user-study descriptions conflict. The main text and Figure 7 include EOGS and CoR-GS, whereas Appendix A.2 describes a DFC2019 comparison involving Sat-NeRF, the method without IDU, and the full method, and omits CoR-GS from the GoogleEarth comparison. Presentation randomization, trial allocation, and uncertainty are also unspecified. These discrepancies limit confidence in the precise interpretation of the very high reported preference rates.

Claims of generalization, free-flight navigation, and efficiency exceed the demonstrated scope. Quantitative evaluation covers four Jacksonville areas and four synthetic NYC areas, using fixed orbital elevations. The runtime comparison uses different hardware without specifying matched rendering resolution or Gaussian counts. These results establish a promising block-scale demonstration, but do not yet substantiate broad geographic robustness or a controlled efficiency advantage.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: generating explorable urban scenes from satellite imagery despite missing facade observations. Combining satellite-derived structure with open-domain diffusion priors is practically relevant.

The visual improvements are substantial in the supplied comparisons, particularly for facade appearance and floating artifacts. Quantitative results support improved perceptual quality: FIDCLIP decreases from 87.19 for Mip-Splatting to 27.35 on DFC2019, and from 28.73 for GaussianCity to 9.91 on GoogleEarth.

The progressive viewpoint curriculum is well motivated by the degradation of satellite reconstructions at lower elevations. Tables 3–4 provide initial evidence for the reconstruction regularizers, curriculum, and multiple diffusion samples.

The supplement provides useful implementation details, including camera schedules, prompts, optimization settings, input-image counts, and training costs. The paper also acknowledges computational expense and poor extreme street-level detail.
weaknesses: The evidence supports perceptual improvement more convincingly than the central claims of geometric accuracy and cross-view consistency. CLIP-based distribution metrics and image-quality preferences do not directly establish either property. There is no quantitative depth, surface, reprojection, or temporal-consistency evaluation. Google Earth references also differ from the real satellite captures in acquisition conditions. Plausible hallucinated facades are valuable, but the paper repeatedly describes them as accurate recovered geometry without sufficient validation.

The depth objective is technically inconsistent with its stated purpose. Equation (3) defines Ldepth as the absolute Pearson correlation, which is minimized with a positive coefficient in Equations (4)–(5). This encourages zero correlation rather than agreement between predicted and rendered depths. This could be a transcription error, but the implemented objective needs clarification because depth supervision is a claimed contributor to the results.

The distinct contribution beyond existing render-edit-update pipelines is insufficiently isolated. Most components are adopted from established methods, making the curriculum and multiple-sample strategy especially important. Their ablation covers only JAX_068, lacks the configuration disabling both, and reports no variability across diffusion seeds. A controlled comparison with a conventional IDU schedule using the same initialization, views, and computation would better establish the methodological advance.

The user-study protocol is internally inconsistent. Section 4.1 and Figure 7 report comparisons including EOGS and CoR-GS, whereas Appendix A.2 describes a DFC2019 study involving Sat-NeRF, the method without IDU, and the full method, and omits CoR-GS from the GoogleEarth comparison. These discrepancies leave unclear which alternatives participants actually evaluated. Randomization and uncertainty estimates are also not reported, weakening this major source of supporting evidence.

Several claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Quantitative evaluation covers four Jacksonville and four New York scenes, with the latter using synthetic overhead Google Earth renders; this provides limited evidence for broad geographic robustness. Evaluation uses prescribed orbital trajectories rather than unrestricted ground-level navigation. Rendering-speed comparisons use different hardware without specifying matched resolution or scene complexity. Finally, the claim of outperforming every baseline on every metric is contradicted by DFC2019 SSIM: CoR-GS achieves 0.350 versus 0.321 for the proposed method. These issues collectively favor weak rejection despite the promising visual results.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: creating explorable urban scenes from satellite imagery without requiring scene-specific street-level observations or 3D annotations. The combination of satellite-derived structure and open-domain generative priors is practically appealing.

The descending-view curriculum is well motivated by the progressive degradation of satellite-trained reconstructions at lower elevations. Appearance modeling, geometric regularization, and iterative diffusion refinement form a coherent pipeline.

The perceptual improvements are substantial. On DFC2019, FIDCLIP improves from 87.19 for Mip-Splatting to 27.35; on GoogleEarth, it improves from 28.73 for GaussianCity to 9.91. Figures 6, 11, and 12 show clearer structures and more plausible facades, while the reported user studies strongly favor the method.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, including prompts, camera schedules, optimization settings, scene coordinates, and approximately seven hours of total processing per scene. The paper also acknowledges computational cost and degraded street-level textures.
weaknesses: The claims of geometrically accurate completion and strong cross-view consistency exceed the evidence. CLIP-based distribution metrics and subjective video preferences primarily establish perceptual plausibility; no direct geometry or cross-view consistency measurements are reported. GoogleEarth provides a consistent synthetic reference that could support stronger geometric evaluation. Hallucinated facade detail should be distinguished from recovery of real structures.

The depth objective is incorrect as written: Equation 3 defines Ldepth as the absolute Pearson correlation, which Equations 4 and 5 minimize with a positive weight. This encourages decorrelation rather than depth agreement. This may be a transcription error, but the implemented objective must be clarified before the depth-supervision results are technically interpretable.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the incremental contribution over existing render-edit-update methods is insufficiently isolated. Most components are established techniques, leaving the curriculum and multiple samples as the main methodological additions. Table 4 supports these choices, but only on JAX_068, without repeated trials or a clearly specified, compute-matched random-view control. Broader controlled comparisons are needed to establish robustness beyond this scene.

Evaluation breadth is limited relative to the free-flight and generalization claims. Quantitative tests cover four Jacksonville scenes and four synthetic New York scenes, using fixed orbital elevations of 17 and 45 degrees. These tests do not establish reliable arbitrary trajectories or street-level navigation; the additional qualitative Jacksonville examples only partly address this limitation.

Several evaluation details undermine reproducibility. Section A.2 describes user-study comparison groups that differ from those in the main text and Figure 7. The patch-count description is ambiguous about aggregation across AOIs, and uncertainty across scenes or stochastic runs is absent. The claim of outperforming every baseline on every metric is also contradicted by DFC2019 SSIM: CoR-GS achieves 0.350 versus 0.321.

The rendering-efficiency comparison uses different hardware without specifying matched resolution, scene complexity, or rendering configuration. The claimed 40 FPS on a MacBook Air uses an unexplained 'fused representation,' making the portability and speed claims difficult to assess. Overall, the promising visual results make this a close decision, but the unresolved technical and evidential issues favor borderline rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: converting sparse, multi-date satellite observations into explorable urban scenes without scene-specific ground-level imagery. Under Algorithms/General, the task-specific integration and demonstrated perceptual improvements support a slight preference for acceptance.

The pipeline is well motivated. Appearance modeling addresses illumination changes, opacity and depth regularization improve initialization, and progressively lowering refinement viewpoints provides a sensible curriculum for exposing facades. Existing components, including WildGaussians, FlowEdit, and iterative dataset updates, are appropriately acknowledged.

The perceptual evidence is substantial across eight quantitatively evaluated scenes. DFC2019 FIDCLIP improves from 84.95 for the strongest reported baseline to 27.03, while GoogleEarth improves from 16.09 to 10.29. Qualitative comparisons show noticeably cleaner structures and richer facades, and the two 44-participant studies strongly favor the proposed method.

The ablations provide useful supporting evidence: curriculum refinement improves FIDCLIP from 33.79 to 28.35, and reconstruction-stage regularization reduces LiDAR DSM MAE from 3.542 m to 2.250 m. The supplement supplies substantial implementation detail, additional architectures, prompt variations, resource measurements, and a two-block scalability demonstration.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about geometric accuracy and cross-view consistency exceed the quantitative evidence. LiDAR evaluation covers reconstruction-stage variants on one AOI, without measuring whether subsequent diffusion refinement preserves or improves geometry. FIDCLIP, CMMD, and human preferences establish perceptual plausibility but do not directly establish accurate facade geometry or temporal consistency. Geometry measurements before and after synthesis across multiple AOIs would materially strengthen the central claim.

The main algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: the framework combines established appearance modeling, monocular-depth regularization, FlowEdit, and iterative dataset updates, with an elevation curriculum and multiple samples per view. The curriculum and SDEdit comparisons are helpful, but synthesis ablations cover only JAX_068 and report no uncertainty across random seeds. Consequently, the general benefit of the proposed additions is less established than the overall pipeline's benefit.

The explanation that independently generated samples promote a geometrically coherent consensus is heuristic. Optimizing against several inconsistent images can also smooth or compromise conflicting details; it does not explicitly enforce correspondence or select mutually consistent samples. The distribution-metric ablation supports a practical benefit but does not directly validate the proposed cross-view-consistency mechanism.

The evaluation has important scope limitations. Real satellite experiments are concentrated in Jacksonville; NYC inputs are synthetic Google Earth renders. Reference imagery differs in illumination and potentially scene content from the real satellite observations, as acknowledged. Moreover, orbit-based evaluation at 17° and 45° provides limited quantitative support for unrestricted street-level navigation. The additional qualitative scenes and reported free-flight videos broaden the evidence but do not fully resolve these limitations.

Some technical and reporting details need clarification. Equation 3 minimizes one minus the absolute depth correlation, so reversed depth ordering can also minimize the loss. Equation 2 sums opacity entropy over all Gaussians without specifying normalization, leaving its effective scale ambiguous as densification changes their number. Claims of consistently best performance should also be qualified: Mip-Splatting has better average GoogleEarth LPIPS and lower CMMD in two of its four scenes. These issues do not negate the perceptual contribution, but they affect technical precision and reproducibility.

strengths: Under Algorithms/General, the paper offers a useful, coherent contribution to satellite-conditioned 3D scene synthesis. Combining satellite reconstruction with progressively lower-view diffusion refinement addresses a meaningful gap between overhead reconstruction and visually plausible facade synthesis.

Perceptual improvements are substantial: DFC2019 FIDCLIP decreases from the strongest baseline's 84.95 to 27.03, and GoogleEarth FIDCLIP improves from 16.09 to 10.29. Qualitative comparisons support reduced floaters and sharper facades. Two studies with 44 participants each provide complementary evidence of strong human preference.

The ablations support several design choices. Table 3 reports improved reconstruction-stage LiDAR DSM errors, while Table 4 supports curriculum scheduling and multiple diffusion samples. Comparisons with SDEdit and prompt-sensitivity experiments go beyond simply demonstrating the complete pipeline.

The supplement provides substantial implementation detail, per-scene results, resource measurements, and additional examples. The portable Gaussian representation and multi-block demonstration add practical value. Overall, the demonstrated synthesis gains support a slight preference for acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: Evidence for geometric accuracy is substantially weaker than evidence for visual plausibility. The LiDAR evaluation concerns initial reconstruction on one AOI, rather than geometry after diffusion refinement. CLIP distribution metrics and human judgments cannot establish accurate hidden facades or cross-view correspondence. Final-stage geometry evaluation and measurements of satellite-view fidelity would better support the repeated claims of preserved, accurate geometry.

Ground-level and unrestricted navigation claims exceed the quantitative evaluation. Refinement cameras descend only to 45 degrees, and benchmark trajectories use 17-degree or 45-degree orbital views. The supplement references withheld free-flight videos, but these are not included in the supplied PDF. Coverage measured against the final model also cannot detect missing surfaces, as the authors acknowledge.

The algorithmic novelty is primarily the curriculum and integration of existing components: WildGaussians appearance modeling, monocular depth supervision, IDU, and FlowEdit. Although random-view and SDEdit ablations are useful, comparisons with fixed low-elevation refinement or an adapted existing diffusion-guided 3D refinement pipeline would better isolate the contribution beyond applying a strong image editor.

Key synthesis ablations use only JAX_068 and report no seed variability. Increasing diffusion samples from one to two nearly doubles reported runtime, without a compute-matched control. Consequently, the experiments do not fully separate benefits of multiple samples from additional computation, and the proposed cross-view consensus explanation remains heuristic.

Evaluation and reporting need clarification. GoogleEarth inputs and references come from the same rendered environment, limiting evidence of real-satellite generalization beyond Jacksonville. Patch counts are ambiguous: 30 frames per AOI times 144 patches gives 4,320 patches per AOI, not across four AOIs. Claims of consistently best performance also overlook several metric and scene-level exceptions.

Equation 3 minimizes one minus absolute depth correlation, so perfectly reversed depth ordering receives the same loss as correct ordering. This ambiguity should be justified or corrected. It does not by itself invalidate the empirical results, but weakens the stated geometric rationale.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General category, the paper presents a useful contribution to satellite-conditioned urban scene synthesis. Its integration of satellite reconstruction, diffusion refinement, and progressive viewpoint selection addresses a meaningful gap between overhead reconstruction and visually convincing close-range exploration, without requiring task-specific training on street-level imagery.

The perceptual improvements are substantial, especially on real satellite imagery. On DFC2019, FIDCLIP improves from the strongest baseline's 84.95 to 27.03, and CMMD from 4.788 to 2.110. Figure 7 shows visibly cleaner building boundaries and more plausible facades. Two studies with 44 participants each provide complementary evidence, with approximately 90–94% preference on DFC2019 and 79–82% on GoogleEarth.

The main design choices receive meaningful experimental support. Table 3 reports improved reconstruction-stage LiDAR DSM errors, with MAE decreasing from 3.542 m to 2.250 m. Table 4 supports curriculum sampling, multiple diffusion samples, and FlowEdit refinement over the tested alternatives. Supplementary prompt variations, additional scenes, and a combined two-block experiment strengthen the empirical case.

The method is described with useful implementation detail, including camera schedules, prompts, optimization settings, input counts, and resource requirements. The portable Gaussian representation and reported interactive rendering make the output practically useful. Prior methods and datasets are broadly attributed, and the limitations concerning off-nadir inputs and occluded viewpoints are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The evidence supports perceptual plausibility more strongly than the repeated claims of accurate recovered geometry and satellite-to-ground consistency. LiDAR evaluation is restricted to reconstruction-stage ablations on one AOI; it does not establish that diffusion refinement preserves or improves final geometry. CLIP distribution metrics and human judgments cannot fully resolve this distinction. Final-stage geometric evaluation and measurements of retained satellite-view fidelity would materially strengthen these claims.

The originality is primarily in the task-specific integration and curriculum, since appearance modeling, monocular depth supervision, FlowEdit, and iterative dataset updates are adopted from existing work. The random-view and SDEdit ablations are useful, but comparisons against stronger alternative schedules using the same diffusion editor and matched computational budgets would better establish the contribution of the proposed curriculum. Similarly, multiple independent samples provide a useful heuristic, but their photometric aggregation does not itself guarantee cross-view consistency.

Evaluation breadth remains limited relative to the claims of generalization and unrestricted exploration. Quantitative results cover four Jacksonville AOIs and four NYC scenes; the NYC inputs are Google Earth renders rather than satellite acquisitions. Standard evaluations use fixed-elevation orbits, while the supplementary text references free-flight videos that are not available in the supplied PDF. The geographic and trajectory evidence therefore supports block-scale oblique-view synthesis more convincingly than broad street-level navigation.

Equation 3 minimizes one minus the absolute Pearson correlation, so perfectly reversed depth ordering receives the same loss as correct ordering. For depth predictions differing by a positive scale and shift, this sign ambiguity is unjustified. The paper should explain this choice or test signed correlation; the reported empirical improvements do not eliminate the objective's degeneracy.

Several conclusions should be calibrated to the mixed results and experimental scope. Mip-Splatting has better average LPIPS on GoogleEarth and better distribution metrics on scene 219, despite table captions claiming consistently best performance. Ablations on a single AOI lack uncertainty estimates, and runtime comparisons across different hardware do not isolate method efficiency. These reservations limit the strength of the claims, but do not outweigh the demonstrated perceptual contribution.
